draft.title: Reliability, validity and bias
card: Reliable
research gives consistent results. If another researcher repeated it in the same way, they would expect to get similar findings.
Valid
research measures what it claims to measure. A study can give the same result every time and still be invalid if it measures the wrong thing.
Bias
is a leaning that pushes results in one direction. It can come from the researcher, such as their own opinions, or from the method, such as leading questions or a sample that leaves out some groups.
Researchers watch for bias by using neutral wording, choosing a sample that reflects the group they study, and being open about their own views.
draft.remember: Reliable means consistent, valid means accurate to the aim, and bias can weaken both.

a.q: A researcher repeats a survey on student sleep with the same students and gets very similar results. Which quality does this show?
opts: Reliability
Validity
Bias
Confidentiality
a.why: Getting similar results when the research is repeated shows it is reliable. It does not show validity, because consistent results could still come from measuring the wrong thing.
a.clue: Think about getting the same result again.

b.q: Jaya wants to study how much time teenagers spend with friends. Her questionnaire asks, "Don't you agree that teens waste too much time online?" What is the main problem?
opts: Bias, because the wording leads respondents to agree
Low reliability, because the same people answered twice
Low validity, because the sample was too small
No problem, because the results would be consistent
b.why: The wording pushes respondents towards one answer, which is bias in the method. Consistent results would not fix this, because a leading question can give the same skewed answers every time.
b.clue: Look at how the question is worded.

b.best: Bias, because the wording leads respondents to agree

problems.detail: Jaya wants to measure time spent with friends, but her question asks about time online. That is also a validity problem: it measures the wrong thing. The scenario mixes two flaws, so a careful student may hesitate between bias and validity. The validity option only fails because of its unrelated reason about sample size. The question should ask about something on topic, for example 'Don't you agree teens spend too much time with friends?'

'Bias can weaken both' says something the card does not teach. The card never links bias to reliability. Why (b) also says a leading question can give the same skewed answers every time, which means biased results can still be reliable. So the remember line contradicts the explanation.

check.summary: Question b's scenario also contains a validity flaw, because the question asks about online time when Jaya is studying time with friends, so the intended answer is muddied. The remember line's claim that bias weakens reliability is not taught on the card and conflicts with why (b).
